title: The mosque of palm trunks
hook: in Medina the Prophet's Mosque is built of mud brick and palm, and he carries bricks

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quba, the first mosque, stones carried by the Prophet himself. Your line was lift a stone too. Did you do the shared chore? Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Today in Medina, the Prophet's Mosque is enormous. White marble, a sea of columns, air conditioning, room for many hundreds of thousands of people, green dome over his grave. Pilgrims come from every country on earth. But stand in it and try to picture the first version. A patch of ground where dates were laid out to dry. A wall of sun-dried mud brick about head height. Tree trunks for pillars. Palm branches for a roof, which leaked when it rained. A floor of earth and pebbles. And among the people carrying the bricks from the kiln, sweating in the heat, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself. Today: the mosque of palm trunks.
screen: `MARBLE AND A GREEN DOME.` → `MUD, PALM, PEBBLES.` → `HE CARRIED BRICKS.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari. When the Prophet reached the center of Medina, the land where his camel knelt belonged to two orphan boys. They offered it to him as a gift. He insisted on paying for it. The plot had some palm trees and some old graves. The trees were cut down, and their trunks lined up to make the pillars. The walls went up in mud brick. The roof was palm leaves laid over beams. And the companions carried the bricks, chanting a short rhyming verse as they worked, and the Prophet carried bricks with them and chanted along. It was built plainly, and on purpose. It had to be. There was no money. But even later, when there was, the mosque stayed simple for a long time. A floor of pebbles, so that when it rained, people prayed in mud. A hadith even describes the Prophet rising from prostration at the dawn prayer one Ramadan with mud and water on his forehead. And one palm trunk has its own story. Before there was a pulpit, the Prophet used to lean against a trunk when he gave the Friday sermon. When a small wooden pulpit was built and he stepped up onto it, Sahih al-Bukhari says the trunk cried out, like a child, and the Prophet came down and put his hand on it until it quieted. The house of God, in Medina, began as the plainest building in town. Everything that came later was built on that.
screen: `TWO ORPHANS' LAND, PAID FOR.` · `TRUNKS FOR PILLARS, PALM FOR A ROOF.` · `A FLOOR OF PEBBLES AND MUD.` · `THE TRUNK THAT CRIED.` · then, large: `BUILT PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit on the floor for this session. If you can, get down there now. No cushion needed, or just a thin one. Feel how close you are to the ground. This is how the first Muslims prayed in that mosque, on earth and pebbles, shoulder to shoulder. Notice what it's like to have nothing between you and the floor but your own clothes. Let it be plain. The bell holds the time.
The mosque of palm trunks. The first Prophet's Mosque in Medina: mud brick, palm pillars, a palm-leaf roof, and a floor of pebbles. Today's word.
screen: `THE MOSQUE OF PALM TRUNKS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: built plainly. Today, choose the plain version of one thing: the simple meal, the short message, the outfit you don't have to think about. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: The Prophet's Mosque in Medina is the second holiest mosque for Muslims, and many pilgrims visit it; many local mosques around the world are still simple rooms, often with carpets on the floor and no furniture.

fork.setup: two orphan boys offer you their land for the new mosque, free. you're the leader of the whole community. what do you do?
options: insist on paying them for it.
fork.reveal: he insisted on paying the orphans. even the house of God wasn't built on a child's loss.

original.note: Arabic: the Prophet's Mosque, in Medina.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grand mosque from the start.
what it means: mud brick, palm-trunk pillars, a palm-leaf roof, a pebble floor, built by everyone, the Prophet among them.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 428 gives the build, 3583 the crying trunk (hanin al-jidh'), a story narrated by many companions.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 428; 3906 (the land, the orphans, the building)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2016 (mud on his forehead in Ramadan)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3583, 3584 (the palm trunk that cried)

notes: The orphans are named Sahl and Suhayl in Bukhari 3906; the script leaves the names out. Bukhari 428 says the land was offered free and the Prophet bought it; confirm the retelling.
'A patch of ground where dates were laid out to dry' (a mirbad) follows the sirah; confirm.
Modern capacity of the mosque stated loosely ('many hundreds of thousands'); confirm or soften.
Bukhari 2016 places the mud on his forehead at the dawn prayer on the twenty-first of Ramadan; the script now says 'at the dawn prayer one Ramadan'. Confirm.
